sources.label: NCERT: work experience and vocational education

pyqs.question: Write one objective of Work Education.
answer: One objective is to develop the dignity of labour — so that a child who sweeps the classroom or works in the garden does it without embarrassment, and treats the sweeper, cook and gardener as members of the school.

pyqs.question: Mention the four pillars of education.
answer: Learning to know, learning to do, learning to live together and learning to be. These four pillars are UNESCO's formulation, set out in the Delhi Declaration of 1969 and developed in the Faure Report, Learning to Be (1972).

pyqs.question: Write one difference between work education and vocational education.
answer: Work education is education through work, for every child, aiming at dignity of labour and self-reliance. Vocational education is education for a specific trade, for a selected group, leading to certification and placement. They differ in purpose, not only in timing.

pyqs.question: What is work in work education?
answer: Work, as this syllabus uses the word, means planned activities carried out to produce, maintain, improve, innovate or transform materials, facilities, living conditions or services, with the specific purpose of meeting needs of conservation or extension, in socially approved ways.

pyqs.question: What is bagless day?
answer: A bagless day is a day in the school programme when children come without bags, books and notebooks and spend the day in activity instead — visiting, working, observing and discussing — so that learning happens through experience.

pyqs.question: Mention one objective of vocational education.
answer: To equip the learner with the knowledge, skills and attitudes required for a specific occupation, to a standard an employer will recognise, so that the training ends in certification and a placement in that trade.

pyqs.question: Define Vocational Education.
answer: Vocational education is education for a vocation — a specific occupation or trade — equipping the learner with the knowledge, skills and attitudes needed to enter and perform that work to a standard an employer will recognise, normally leading to a certificate.

pyqs.question: Write a short note: NEP 2020 and work education.
answer:
NEP 2020 and work education
NEP 2020 replaces the old 10 per cent vocationalisation reservation with vocational exposure from Grade 6 onwards, so that no child is routed out of the mainstream at fourteen. It adopts the 5+3+3+4 design, makes work education a dimension of every subject rather than a separate stream, and aims that every child has at least one vocational skill by the end of the school stage.

pyqs.question: Write a short note: View of Mahatma Gandhi regarding work education.
answer:
Mahatma Gandhi and work education
In Hind Swaraj (1909) Gandhi identified the village and the charkha as the soul of India and attacked the division between bookish and manual education. Nai Talim (1918–19) centred the whole of education on productive manual craft. Two convictions run through it: all work is dignified, and education should be self-supporting.

pyqs.question: Write a short note: Differences between work education and vocational education.
answer:
Work education and vocational education
Work education is education through work — integrated with the whole curriculum, for every child without selection, broad in outcome and normally uncertified. Vocational education is education for a specific trade, with a separate syllabus, for a selected group from the secondary stage, ending in certification and placement.

pyqs.question: Write a short note: Kothari Commission and Work Education.
answer:
Kothari Commission and work education
The Education Commission, chaired by Dr. D. S. Kothari, was set up in 1964 and submitted its report on 29 June 1966. It recommended ten years of general education as 7+3+2, that work experience and national service should form an integral part of the educational programme in every institution, and a 10 per cent reservation for vocationalisation at the secondary stage. The National Policy on Education of 1968 carried this language into official policy.

pyqs.question: Write a short note: Mahatma Gandhi and work education.
answer:
Mahatma Gandhi and work education
In Hind Swaraj (1909) Gandhi argued that the village and the charkha were the soul of India and criticised sharply the division between bookish and manual education. From this came Nai Talim (1918–19), in which the whole of education was centred on productive manual craft. Vinoba Bhave and the Shramdan movement carried it into institutional practice. What survives in policy is the principle — dignity of labour and education connected to the means of living.

pyqs.question: Write a short note: Four pillars of education.
answer:
Four pillars of education
Learning to know, learning to do, learning to live together and learning to be — UNESCO's four pillars, from the Delhi Declaration of 1969 and the Faure Report, Learning to Be (1972). One work activity can serve all four: measuring a plot for a seed bed teaches knowing, cooking and building teach doing, group production teaches living together, and choosing a material and judging one's own finished work teaches being.

pyqs.question: Write a short note: Mahatma Gandhi and Work Education.
answer: Mahatma Gandhi and Work Education

Gandhi's educational thought grew out of his political argument. In Hind Swaraj (1909) he argued that the village and the charkha were the soul of India, and that independence could not be built by a small elite but had to begin among the millions who work with their hands. From this came basic education, or Nai Talim, usually dated 1918-19 and developed around the Non-Cooperation movement, in which the whole of education from the earliest stage upward was centred on productive manual craft with the charkha at its heart. Two convictions run through it: all work is dignified, and education should be self-supporting, so that the products are useful enough to pay for the process. Vinoba Bhave and the Shramdan movement carried the scheme into institutional practice. A small rural Assamese school running a kitchen garden or a paper and stationery unit is a standing example of what he meant.

practice: What makes a work activity educational?
It has a planned learning purpose and connects practical action with understanding, skills or values.
Define dignity of labour.
Dignity of labour means respecting useful work and the people who perform it, regardless of its social status or whether it is manual.
What is learning by doing?
Learning by doing develops understanding through purposeful activity and reflection on the experience.
What is self-reliance in work education?
Self-reliance is the growing ability to perform suitable tasks responsibly and seek help appropriately when needed.
What is craft-centred learning?
Craft-centred learning uses a meaningful craft activity as a basis for connecting practical work with knowledge and values.
Name the thinker associated with Nai Talim.
Mahatma Gandhi.
Name the educational work associated with Rousseau's discussion of education through experience.
Émile, or On Education.
What is vocational exposure?
Vocational exposure introduces learners to different kinds of work and skills so they can understand possible occupations.
What does SUPW stand for?
Socially Useful Productive Work.
Which pillar of education emphasises cooperation with others?
Learning to live together.
State two educational benefits of making a useful classroom object.
Planning and making the object connects ideas such as measurement with practical decisions.
Using and reviewing it develops responsibility for the quality and usefulness of one's work.
Distinguish work education from using work as punishment.
Work education is planned for learning and shared fairly, with safe, age-appropriate participation.
Punitive work is imposed to cause discomfort or shame; it undermines respect for the task and for those who do it.
How can work education challenge gender stereotypes?
Offer all learners access to different tasks, such as gardening, stitching and organising materials, without assigning them by gender.
Discuss the skills required and recognise everyone's contribution rather than describing work as naturally belonging to boys or girls.
Explain the connection between practical activity and understanding.
Practical activity gives learners concrete evidence to examine, such as how a folded paper shape changes.
Discussion and reflection connect what happened with an idea, so doing an activity is followed by understanding it.
Give two reasons to include local occupations in school learning.
Local occupations provide familiar examples of how knowledge and skills are used outside school.
Meeting workers respectfully can broaden learners' understanding of community contributions and possible future interests.
Why is the finished product not the only purpose of work education?
Learners also develop planning, cooperation, safe working habits and problem-solving during the process.
An imperfect product can still show meaningful learning, while an adult-made product may reveal little about the learner's own development.
How does a work activity support learning to know?
Learners investigate the materials and ideas involved, such as what seeds need to germinate.
They use observations and explanations to understand the activity instead of merely following instructions.
How does a work activity support learning to do?
It gives learners guided opportunities to practise a practical skill, such as measuring and folding paper accurately.
Feedback and repeated attempts help them apply knowledge more effectively in a real task.
Explain learning to be through one work-education example.
Learning to be concerns personal development, judgement and responsibility.
A learner who plans, completes and reviews a manageable task can develop independence and confidence while recognising when help is needed.
Why should introductory vocational experiences remain broad?
Broad experiences let learners explore different interests and recognise many forms of skilled work.
They avoid confining a child prematurely to an occupation because of family background, gender or an adult's assumption.
Explain three objectives of work education beyond earning money.
Connect school knowledge with practical situations so learning becomes meaningful.
Develop useful skills and responsible habits through supervised activity.
Build cooperation and respect for workers by recognising the effort and expertise involved in different tasks.
A lesson only asks learners to copy the names of craft tools. Suggest three changes inspired by craft-centred learning.
Begin with a suitable useful task and introduce tools through their actual purpose rather than a list alone.
Connect the supervised activity with ideas such as measurement and material properties, asking learners to explain their choices.
Reflect on cooperation, resource use and the value of the work, joining practical activity with understanding and responsibility.
Describe three learning opportunities in observing a local craftsperson.
Learners can identify the materials and stages of production and ask why a method is used.
They can connect the work with classroom ideas such as shape, measurement or material properties.
They can recognise the craftsperson's expertise and reflect on how the work contributes to community life.
How is purposeful work different from mechanical repetition?
Purposeful work has a learning goal understood by the learners.
It requires attention to decisions and results, rather than repeating a movement without understanding.
Reflection allows learners to explain difficulties and improve their approach, turning experience into learning.
State three conditions for selecting an educational work activity.
It should fit a clear learning goal and be suitable for the learners' age and needs.
Materials, tools and supervision must make participation safe and accessible.
The activity should offer meaningful involvement and reflection rather than leaving most learners watching one person work.
Explain how vocational education can support informed career choices.
It introduces the knowledge and skills used in occupational fields.
Practical experience helps learners recognise interests and areas in which they need further training.
Information about qualifications and working conditions helps them consider choices realistically rather than relying on stereotypes.
A school reserves practical work only for pupils labelled weak in studies. Critique this arrangement in light of work experience as part of general education.
Work experience was recommended as an integral part of general education, so restricting it to a labelled group misses its broad educational purpose.
The arrangement can reinforce an unfair divide between intellectual and practical ability and stigmatise manual work.
Provide meaningful, accessible work experiences for all learners and connect them with classroom understanding, adapting support rather than excluding pupils.
How can a school connect a bagless activity with learning?
Set a learning purpose before the activity, such as understanding how a potter selects and shapes material.
Arrange safe observation, questions and appropriate hands-on participation with supervision.
Afterwards, help learners discuss or record what they learned and connect it with classroom concepts.
Explain the place of experience in Rousseau's educational thinking.
Rousseau criticised relying only on verbal instruction and book knowledge.
He emphasised learning through experience and engagement with the environment, taking the child's development into account.
Practical work can therefore be read as a means of developing understanding and independence, rather than simply preparing a product.
Why should work education be available to every learner?
Practical understanding and everyday responsibilities are useful to all learners.
Shared participation challenges the belief that manual work belongs only to particular social groups.
Adapted tasks allow learners with different abilities to contribute and develop skills rather than being excluded or labelled.
Illustrate the four pillars of learning through a school gardening activity.
Learning to know: investigate the conditions plants need and explain observations.
Learning to do: practise suitable tasks such as measuring spacing and watering carefully.
Learning to live together: share responsibilities, listen to suggestions and solve group disagreements.
Learning to be: develop responsibility and judgement by caring for plants and reviewing one's own contribution.
Compare work education and vocational education without treating either as inferior.
Work education uses purposeful work for broad learning, practical habits and values within education.
Vocational education gives more focused preparation in knowledge and skills related to occupational areas.
Their emphasis differs, but both can combine understanding, practical ability and responsible attitudes.

A general gardening project may develop cooperation and observation, while vocational horticultural study develops more specialised competence. Neither should be assigned on the assumption that some learners are unfit for academic learning.
Explain how a paper-making activity could become craft-centred learning.
Begin with a useful purpose, such as making a small notebook, and discuss suitable materials.
Connect preparation with measurement, counting and estimation of paper use.
During making, ask learners to explain choices and solve practical problems with guidance.
Review the notebook's usefulness, resource use and cooperation. These links make the craft a means of learning rather than an isolated decorative exercise.
Explain four ways to promote dignity of labour at school.
Speak respectfully about all workers and recognise the skill and effort in their work.
Share suitable classroom responsibilities fairly rather than allocating them by caste, gender or status.
Invite community workers to explain their expertise and encourage thoughtful questions.
Ensure activities are safe and educational, never humiliating or substitutes for hazardous adult work. Respect for labour must include respect for the person doing it.
Identify four weaknesses in a work programme based only on copying a model.
Learners may follow steps without understanding why the method works.
Identical outcomes can discourage creativity and adaptation to local needs.
A focus on neatness can hide differences in effort, cooperation and independent learning.
Without discussion or review, errors may be corrected mechanically rather than used for problem-solving. Add choices, explanations and reflection to improve the programme.
Design a school work-education programme grounded in meaningful learning.
Identify relevant needs and learning goals with learners and staff, such as organising a class library.
Choose safe, accessible tasks that link knowledge with practical action and offer different ways to contribute.
Plan materials, time, supervision and responsibilities, inviting suitable community expertise where useful.
Provide demonstrations, guided practice and opportunities for learners to make and explain decisions.
Assess understanding, skills, cooperation and the result through observation and reflection. Use the findings to improve the next activity, keeping learning rather than output alone at the centre.
Discuss how work education can connect school, home and community.
Select tasks connected with familiar needs, such as caring for plants, maintaining books or reducing material waste.
Invite learners to share relevant home experiences without assuming all families have the same resources or occupations.
Involve willing community members as knowledge partners and recognise their expertise respectfully.
Connect practical experiences with classroom ideas through discussion, measurement, records and explanation.

Review what learners can apply in safe everyday situations and seek feedback from participants. Community involvement should support learning without placing compulsory financial or labour demands on families.
Explain why education should connect intellectual and practical work.
Practical situations give ideas a concrete purpose, such as using measurement to make an object fit.
Planning and troubleshooting require reasoning, showing that manual work also involves thought.
Testing an idea against a result reveals misunderstandings and creates opportunities to revise explanations.
Combining discussion with action develops communication, cooperation and responsibility alongside practical skill.
It also challenges status divisions between forms of knowledge. A balanced education values understanding and skilled action without reducing learners to either academic or manual categories.
Plan an inclusive vocational-exposure visit.
Choose a suitable workplace or demonstration that supports a clear learning goal and can accommodate all learners.
Discuss access, consent, supervision and safe boundaries with the host; learners should not enter hazardous work areas.
Prepare accessible questions about materials, skills and the worker's contribution, avoiding assumptions based on gender or background.
During the visit, provide meaningful observation and suitable participation, with alternatives where direct handling is not appropriate.
Follow up through discussion or a record of learning, linking the experience to school subjects and future interests. Evaluate participation as well as factual recall.
Evaluate the statement: 'Work education is only a break from academic subjects.'
The statement overlooks work education's planned learning goals and its place in a balanced curriculum.
Activities can apply concepts from mathematics, science and language to meaningful tasks.
They also develop practical skill, cooperation, responsibility and respect for labour, which a break alone does not necessarily teach.
However, an unplanned activity without explanation or reflection may have limited educational value; merely keeping learners busy is insufficient.
A strong programme therefore connects action with inquiry and review. Enjoyment is welcome, but the learning purpose distinguishes work education from time away from study.

pyqs.question: Mention four activities of work education which helps in skill development of the learner.
answer:
- Making stationery items — measuring card, cutting on a board, folding and binding a register — trains precision and sequence.
- Bamboo and clay work — splitting green bamboo, weaving, kneading and shaping — trains hand skill and strength.
- Gardening and plantation — sowing, thinning, watering, planting and keeping a dated garden record — trains care and regularity.
- Cookery and food preservation — cutting, cooking and jarring jam or pickle — trains hygiene, measurement and discipline over a process.

pyqs.question: Write a short note: Population Education and removal of evil customs from the society.
answer:
Population education and removal of evil customs
Population education builds an understanding of population size, growth and distribution and of their relation to family welfare and resources, so that family size becomes a responsible choice. Customs such as child marriage, dowry and caste restriction grow out of ignorance; they are removed by awareness through schools, adult education and women's education, and by enforcing the existing legal provisions against them.

pyqs.question: What do you understand by behavioural change of learner? Write with example.
answer:
A behavioural change is a lasting change in what a child actually does — punctuality, care of tools, responsibility, self-confidence, cooperation — brought about by repeated work under real conditions, not by a single demonstration.
For example: before the programme a girl would not speak in front of the class; in the sixth week she told the group, unprompted, that the knives must be washed before the vegetables are cut because otherwise the food is not safe, and the other eleven children accepted it.

pyqs.question: Write a short note: Behavioural changes in learners through work education activities.
answer: The changes expected are punctuality and regularity, disciplined work habits, respect for tools and materials, responsibility and accountability, self-confidence, problem-solving, cooperation, tolerance of hard work and delayed reward, and a reduced fear of manual work. These are not assertions but records. A child who earlier arrived after the bell and left first now arrives before it, because the garden duty begins then, and signs the duty register for three consecutive weeks without a reminder.

pyqs.question: Mention four activities of work education which help in knowledge and skill development of learners.
answer:
- Raising vegetables in the school garden — measurement, germination and record-keeping happen by doing, not from a diagram.
- Preparing the household budget — bills, addition, percentages and a bar graph become a real plan the family will follow.
- Surveying household waste — weighing, totalling and converting to percentages gives the class its own first dataset.
- Repairing school equipment — the child identifies the material, the force that broke it and the cost of repair against replacement.

pyqs.question: “Work education promotes humanistic values of students” — Justify.
answer: Humanistic values are the dispositions that treat other people as ends in themselves. Work education promotes them in a way few subjects can, because the child meets them as a worker rather than as a reader.

- Dignity of labour. The teacher treats the sweeper, cook, gardener and watchman as members of the school and names their work aloud. The worth of an activity is not measured by the social rank of the person who does it.
- Honesty and accountability. A group that keeps accounts and a tool register, and reports honestly when a material is short, is learning a moral habit as much as a clerical one.
- Self-respect. A task graded to the child's present capacity gives the experience of having managed something difficult, and out of that grows an honest self-image as a capable person.
- Regard for others. Group production forces sharing, negotiation over scarce tools and acceptance of a common standard.
- Care for the world. Measuring the water, tending a living plant without owning it, repairing rather than replacing - these make a child someone who maintains rather than merely consumes.

pyqs.question: What is behavioural changes in learners? Mention two activities of work education for elementary learners to develop Social skills.
answer: Behavioural change in learners means a visible and lasting change in what a child does, knows and feels - in the syllabus's three categories, knowledge, skills and attitude. It is not a change in marks alone. It is punctuality, care of tools, cooperation, self-confidence, acceptance of responsibility and a reduced fear of manual work. The test is simple: the teacher must be able to illustrate it with something that actually happened, with a date, rather than merely assert that the child has become disciplined.
Two activities for elementary learners:

1. Group production with divided roles - making eighty file covers, or cooking a dish together. Each child takes one job, scarce tools must be shared fairly, and the product has to meet a common standard. A Class V child who quarrels over who does what in week one can, by week six, describe what the whole group did.

2. A shared school responsibility - the published daily cleanliness rota, or the garden duty. Because the rota names every child and everybody serves, a learner learns that the tidiness of the school is not the sweeper's business alone.

pyqs.question: Write a short note: Sociocultural evils.
answer: Socio-cultural evils

These are the customs, practices and beliefs of a society that harm the well-being of its members - untouchability and the caste-based division of labour, the idea that certain occupations are beneath certain people, the exclusion of girls, child labour and child marriage, and the neglect of the old and the sick. They persist because the work behind them is invisible, done by one person, and therefore never discussed. Work education attacks them directly by teaching the dignity of labour. When a child sweeps without embarrassment and speaks of the sweeper as 'we', the social division of work has lost its moral base.

pyqs.question: What is socio-cultural evils? What is the role of learners social skill development in removing social evils?
answer: Socio-cultural evils are the customs, practices and beliefs of a society that harm the well-being of its members - untouchability and the caste-based division of labour, the belief that certain work is beneath certain people, the exclusion of girls, child labour, child marriage, and the neglect of the old and the sick. They survive because the work they justify is invisible, being done by one person, and therefore never discussed.

Social skill development is the direct answer. Social skills are the habits of living with other people - cooperating, sharing, resolving conflict, showing respect and holding an honest self-image. UNESCO's third pillar, learning to live together, names the same thing, and work education builds it through its very nature. Group production with divided roles forces a child to negotiate who does what, to wait for a turn, and to accept a common standard. In a school garden shared across castes and sexes, a child who once called sweeping inferior work begins to say 'we' about the sweeper. That one change of word removes the evil at its root, because a caste division of work rests on the denial of labour's dignity.

pyqs.question: How behavioural changes of learners can be gained through activities of work education? Explain with examples.
answer: Behaviour is learned by repetition under conditions, and that is exactly what a graded work programme supplies. A single exciting demonstration changes almost nothing; a task performed regularly over weeks, with feedback and a real consequence, changes a great deal. The cycle runs: graded and repeated work, then habit, then attitude, then a self-image of 'I am capable', which sends the child back to deeper work.

The changes are observable:
- Punctuality - arriving before the bell because the garden duty begins then.
- Care of tools - scissors sharpened and returned to the register instead of handled as toys.
- Responsibility - accepting the group's mistake and saying which step went wrong.
- Tolerance of delayed reward - watering a seed bed for eight weeks before the first harvest, and still watering it on the last day of term.
- Self-confidence - sequencing the steps aloud while leading a group, and not consulting the teacher until two attempts have failed.
Work that is used, eaten or worn changes children faster than work that is only displayed.

practice: What is a cognitive outcome of work education?
It is a change in knowledge or thinking, such as understanding why a plant needs suitable soil and water.
What is a psychomotor outcome?
It is development in coordinated physical performance, such as folding paper accurately.
What is an affective outcome?
It is development in attitudes or values, such as greater care for shared materials.
Give one observable sign of cooperation during work.
A learner offers a shared tool to a partner when their turn is finished.
Give one observable sign of responsibility.
A learner returns materials to the agreed place after completing a task.
What is perseverance in a practical task?
Perseverance is continuing purposeful effort and trying an improved approach when a task is difficult.
What is hand-eye coordination?
Hand-eye coordination is the coordinated use of visual information to guide hand movements.
What is a baseline observation?
It is a record of a learner's starting performance used for comparison with later observations.
What is a work habit?
A work habit is a regularly practised way of approaching tasks, such as planning materials before starting.
What is transfer of learning?
Transfer of learning is applying understanding or skill learned in one situation to another.
Distinguish learning a fact from developing a work habit.
Learning a fact means gaining knowledge, such as naming a tool's purpose.
Developing a habit means consistently acting in a useful way, such as returning that tool safely after use.
Give two examples of cognitive development through gardening.
A learner explains how too little water affects a plant, using observations.
A learner compares possible causes when seeds fail to germinate rather than guessing without evidence.
Give two examples of skill development through paper craft.
Measuring and marking a required length improves precision in using a ruler.
Folding along a marked line develops controlled hand movements and coordination.
Give two examples of attitude development through a shared task.
Learners show willingness to share tools and assist partners.
They begin to value careful use of materials instead of wasting them or leaving clean-up to others.
Why is one successful performance insufficient evidence of a lasting change?
It may depend on close help, imitation or unusually favourable conditions.
Observing the learner on later occasions and in related tasks gives stronger evidence of consistent development.
How can feedback encourage perseverance?
Describe the useful effort or strategy, such as checking measurements before retrying.
Suggest an achievable next step so the learner knows how to improve instead of hearing only that the result is wrong.
Why should behavioural observations describe actions rather than personality?
An action such as taking turns can be observed and compared over time.
A label such as 'lazy' is a judgement that may overlook barriers and gives little guidance for support.
How can learners practise self-reliance without being left unsupported?
Give a manageable task and let learners attempt appropriate decisions themselves.
Provide help when needed and gradually reduce it as competence grows rather than expecting immediate independence.
State two ways a group task can encourage empathy.
Learners listen to a partner's difficulty and consider what support would help.
Sharing roles lets them appreciate the effort involved in contributions they might otherwise overlook.
What evidence would show transfer of careful material use?
The learner uses paper economically during a taught craft activity.
Later, they apply the same habit to an unfamiliar task, such as planning a display, without needing the same reminder.
Explain knowledge, skill and attitude outcomes of making a notebook.
Knowledge: learners understand the order of stages and why pages need to be aligned.
Skill: they practise measuring, folding and assembling with appropriate tools and support.
Attitude: they care for resources, share responsibilities and persist when the first attempt needs revision.
Explain how a plant-care task can build responsibility.
Agree on a manageable care routine and ensure the learner understands what the plant needs.
Give the learner a meaningful role with appropriate reminders and support.
Review observations together so the learner connects regular care and thoughtful decisions with the plant's condition, rather than merely obeying a schedule.
How can teachers help learners cope constructively with an unsuccessful product?
Treat the result as information about the process rather than proof of the learner's inability.
Help the learner identify a possible cause, such as an inaccurate measurement.
Plan and try a feasible adjustment, then compare the result so persistence is connected with learning.
Describe three signs that teamwork is improving.
Members listen to each other's suggestions before deciding what to do.
Tasks and tools are shared fairly, with support for someone who needs it.
The group resolves disagreements through discussion and accepts shared responsibility for the result.
How can a teacher promote respect for different workers through work education?
Introduce the knowledge and skill required for varied forms of work.
Model respectful language and challenge jokes or stereotypes that demean workers.
Use shared, safe activities and reflection to help learners appreciate contributions without assigning tasks according to social identity.
Explain how choice can support motivation in a work activity.
A limited choice of suitable materials or designs gives learners a sense of participation in the task.
Explaining the purpose helps them connect the work with a meaningful outcome.
Reviewing their own decisions encourages ownership, while guidance keeps the choices safe and manageable.
How should a teacher interpret a learner's reluctance to handle materials?
Observe the situation and ask sensitively about the difficulty instead of assuming unwillingness.
Consider unfamiliarity, fear, access needs or discomfort with the material.
Offer a demonstration, adapted material or alternative role and observe the response before drawing conclusions.
Suggest three ways to record changes in learners' work behaviour.
Use dated observations describing specific actions during tasks.
Keep examples or photographs of work, with appropriate consent and privacy, to show changes in performance.
Include brief learner reflections explaining choices and difficulties, comparing them with observed behaviour.
Why is reflection needed after a practical activity?
It helps learners identify the knowledge and skills they used rather than remembering only the product.
It allows them to examine cooperation, difficulties and choices.
It supports a plan for applying the learning or improving the next attempt.
Explain how a classroom clean-up routine can develop social responsibility.
A shared routine shows that maintaining a usable learning space is a collective responsibility.
Fair, safe roles let learners practise cooperation and care for common resources.
Discussion connects their actions with others' comfort and access; the task should not be used to shame selected children.
Describe how you would document a learner's growing independence.
Identify a specific task and record the help initially needed, such as reminders for each step in organising materials.
Provide suitable guidance and repeated opportunities to practise.
Record later performance, noting whether the learner plans steps, checks work and seeks help appropriately.
Compare similar situations over time and note contextual changes. Independence means informed action with appropriate help-seeking, not refusing all assistance.
Explain the interaction of knowledge, skills and attitudes in work education.
Knowledge helps a learner understand what needs doing and why a method may work.
Practical skill allows the learner to carry out the method with increasing control.
Attitudes such as care and cooperation influence how responsibly the learner uses that ability.
For example, plant care involves understanding needs, watering suitably and maintaining regular responsibility. Strong work education develops these dimensions together.
Plan a small task that develops both problem-solving and cooperation.
Ask groups to create a stable holder for classroom pencils using safe reusable materials.
Invite them to discuss possible designs and divide roles fairly before starting.
Let them test the holder, identify weaknesses and agree on a revision rather than providing an immediate ready-made solution.
Discuss how evidence and listening shaped the final design. Observe both the reasoning used and the way members worked together.
Explain four reasons a work activity may fail to produce intended behavioural changes.
The learning goal may be unclear, leaving learners focused only on finishing.
One learner or adult may do most of the work, so others have little meaningful practice.
Tasks may be inaccessible or too difficult, creating frustration rather than supported development.
Without feedback and later opportunities, new behaviours may not become consistent. Revise participation, support and review rather than blaming learners.
How can teachers assess respect for resources without judging family background?
Use observable criteria such as returning shared materials and choosing appropriate quantities.
Provide equal access to the materials needed, so performance does not depend on what a child can bring from home.
Discuss reasons for a learner's choices before interpreting them as careless or wasteful.
Record progress across tasks and give specific feedback. Avoid equating expensive or polished products with responsible attitudes.
Develop a plan to improve cooperative behaviour through work education.
Identify a specific concern, such as a few learners controlling all shared tools, and record a starting observation.
Choose an accessible group task that genuinely requires contributions from several members.
Model sharing and listening, agree on fair roles and provide support where learners need it.
Observe participation, intervene respectfully when exclusion occurs and invite learners to reflect on how their group worked.
Repeat opportunities and compare later observations with the starting point. Adjust roles and support until cooperation becomes more consistent rather than assuming one successful activity is enough.
Explain how behavioural change should be evaluated over time.
Define the intended change through observable behaviour, such as planning steps before starting.
Record an initial performance and the support available so later comparisons have context.
Gather evidence across several tasks using observation, work samples and learner explanations.
Look for increasing consistency and transfer, while considering differences in task difficulty or assistance.
Use the findings for constructive feedback and new goals. Avoid claiming that the activity alone caused every change or treating one lapse as proof that no learning occurred.
Use a school garden to explain holistic learner development.
Learners investigate plant needs and compare observations, developing understanding and reasoning.
Suitable planting and watering tasks build coordinated practical skills with supervision.
Planning roles and sharing resources provide opportunities for communication and cooperation.
Regular care can develop responsibility and appreciation of the work involved in growing food.

Reflection connects these experiences and helps learners apply them elsewhere. The outcomes depend on inclusive planning and guidance; the presence of a garden alone does not guarantee holistic learning.
Explain how a teacher can encourage perseverance without praising unsafe or pointless persistence.
Help learners identify a meaningful and achievable goal before starting.
When difficulty arises, examine the cause and model how to change strategy rather than repeat the same unsuccessful action.
Offer specific feedback and suitable assistance, recognising progress as well as effort.
Teach learners to stop and seek help when a task is unsafe or beyond their current ability; responsible judgement is part of learning.
Reflect on what the revised approach achieved and what remains to learn. Perseverance is thoughtful continued effort, not enduring harm or refusing support.
Discuss how work education can reduce prejudice about manual work.
Examine stereotypes that rank people by occupation and discuss why they are unfair.
Introduce the planning, knowledge and skill involved in different forms of practical work.
Give all learners fair access to safe, meaningful activities rather than assigning work by gender, caste or perceived academic ability.
Engage respectfully with workers and reflect on their contributions to everyday life.
Observe whether learners' language and behaviour towards others change over time. Practical participation needs explicit reflection and consistent teacher modelling to challenge prejudice.

pyqs.question: Mention two tools used for evaluation of Work Education.
answer: Observation — watching the child at work over a period — and the checklist, a list of yes/no items ticked daily, such as the daily-works checklist for board cleaned, waste separated, garden watered and tools returned.

pyqs.question: What is community resource?
answer: Community resources are the people, places, materials and skills that already exist in a locality — the potter, the field, the pond, bamboo and clay, the panchayat, the health centre. Most of them are free.

pyqs.question: What is human resource?
answer: Human resource means the people of a locality — the potter, weaver, carpenter, farmer, nurse, retired teacher and the parents — whose skills, time and labour a school draws on for its work education programme. Most of it is free.

pyqs.question: Suggest two measures for successful implementation of the subject work education in school.
answer:
- Plan and record properly. A written plan, a materials list, a division of labour and a safety note before the work starts, and a dated record afterwards — date, task, what I noticed, what I did about it. An unrecorded task decays.
- Give the work a real user. The product should be used, eaten, planted, sold or displayed, and the rubric should be published to the children in advance. Work that nobody uses teaches the child that effort does not matter.

pyqs.question: Write a short note: Evaluation system in work education.
answer:
Evaluation system in work education
Evaluation in work education is continuous and comprehensive — a record after every activity, covering both scholastic achievement and the wider development of the learner, with the work activity carrying marks in the internal assessment. The tool must be matched to the claim: a skill is assessed by performance, an attitude by observation and self-report over time, growth by a portfolio or a before-and-after pair, and knowledge by a written or oral test.

pyqs.question: Mention four activities to fulfill the objectives of work education successfully.
answer:
- Run a graded sequence of skills — tearing paper, then folding file covers, then binding a register — so that the child finishes a specified task to a stated standard, unaided.
- Publish a duty roster with a tool register and accounts, so responsibility and accountability are built into the day.
- Set group production with divided roles, shared tools and one common standard, which is what teaches cooperation.
- Take children to real workers — farmers, weavers, artisans — through field visits and resource persons, which prepares them for the world of work.

pyqs.question: Mention the evaluation systems used in work education.
answer: The syllabus asks for continuous and comprehensive evaluation — a short record after every activity, spread across the year and covering skills and attitude as well as marks. The tools are observation, checklist, rating scale, rubric, anecdotal record, interview, questionnaire, practical or performance assessment, portfolio, project report and peer and self-assessment, with the written or oral test reserved for knowledge.

pyqs.question: What is community resource? Prepare a list of community resources of your locality.
answer: A community resource is a person, place, material, organisation or source of information that already exists in a locality and can be used for learning - and most of them are free. Identifying them is a method, not a list: walk the locality, list everything within reach, ask who knows what, and mark what is free, what costs, what needs permission and what is dangerous. A factory, an open well and a road are resources in one sense and hazards in another.

A list for a typical Assamese semi-urban locality:
- People and skills: the potter, weaver, carpenter, blacksmith, mason, cobbler, farmer, midwife, cook, retired teacher, nurse, an NGO worker.
- Places: the paddy field, the pond and river bank, the weekly market, the workshop, the panchayat office, the anganwadi, the health centre, the agricultural office, the library.
- Materials: clay, bamboo, cane, jute, sand, timber offcuts, paddy husk, farmyard manure, crop residue, waste paper, bottles, scrap metal.
- Organisations: the panchayat, the School Management Committee, the Block office, the PWD, the agriculture and forest departments, a cooperative, an NGO.

Utilisation is where most plans fail. Every resource used must be written down with a person responsible, a date, a purpose in one sentence, and a product. Without the product the visit is a trip; with it, it is work.

pyqs.question: Write a short note: Importance of morning assembly in school.
answer: Importance of the morning assembly

The assembly is one of the two compulsory daily works, and it is a small complete piece of organisation - a rehearsal for everything else in this paper.
- Discipline. The group's own members set the standard of standing and silence. A leader who shouts has taught the opposite of what the assembly is for.
- Timekeeping. Ten minutes, never twelve. Appointing a person responsible for time is the most transferable skill in the list.
- Confidence. Every child takes the microphone eventually - prayer, song, thought, announcement - and learns to speak in front of others.
- Community. All classes gather, which is one of the few daily moments when the whole school meets as one.
- Assessment. The three-minute review afterwards against a rating sheet is daily-work assessment in action.

pyqs.question: “Work education is integrated with other curricular subjects” — Justify with examples.
answer: Integration is not co-existence. Co-existence is a separate work period beside the other subjects, and it teaches children that work is what they do when the real lessons are over. Integration means one activity carries objectives from several subjects at once.

Take raising vegetables in the school garden. Language names the plants, writes the labels and reads the seed packet. Mathematics counts plants, measures height, calculates yield per square metre and plots a growth graph. Science observes germination, the needs of a plant and the harm done by insects. Social studies shows where the family's food comes from and who grows it at what cost. Other examples are keeping a household budget, surveying household waste, visiting a food preservation centre and repairing school equipment.
Note what integration does not mean: the activity does not replace language or mathematics teaching. It means the same two periods serve several objectives, which is efficient.

pyqs.question: Discuss about the role of teachers and parents in carrying out different activities of work education in school?
answer: The role of teachers and parents

The syllabus asks the headmaster, teachers and parents to work together through a cycle: identify the need, consult the people affected, plan materials, cost and time, do the work, observe and record, evaluate and improve.

- Teachers carry the classes, work out the sequence, keep the ordinary teaching running alongside, and record what they actually see - which child cannot do what, which material is short, which class is noisy.
- Parents are partners, not visitors. They say plainly what time, labour or money they can actually give, supply materials or labour, and report whether a change has really made a difference at home.
Skipping the consultation stage is the commonest failure. A measure imposed on teachers or on children's homes without asking them is resented, and it is not sustained.

pyqs.question: Explain with examples how the locally available human resources and material resources help in implementation of work education in school.
answer: Work education of the kind this syllabus asks for cannot be bought off a shelf. A school runs the programme out of what the locality already has, and that is a strength — the material is cheap, repairable and familiar.

Human resources come in two groups. Inside the school are the headmaster, who sanctions the plan and keeps the time and the budget; the teachers, who take the classes and record what they observe; and the school's own workers — the cook, the gardener, the sweeper, the watchman. Their work should be named aloud in the timetable, so that the dignity of labour is a fact in the room rather than a line in a textbook. Outside the school there are the potter, the weaver, the carpenter, the farmer, the nurse, the retired teacher. Invite them to demonstrate and to be questioned; the best hour of the year is often the one spent asking a working person about a working day. Parents are partners too, and the School Management Committee is the forum for anything that touches the timetable or the money.

Material resources are cheaper still: clay, bamboo, cane, jute, stone, sand, timber offcuts, coconut husk, paddy husk, farmyard manure, waste paper, bottles, scrap metal. Places count as resources too — the field, the pond, the river bank, the grazing ground, the market — and so do institutions: the panchayat, the Block office, the agriculture office, an NGO.

Three questions settle whether a resource becomes work education: is it locally real, can we actually do it here, and would a child remember the finished thing in five years. Then write it down with four things — a person responsible, a date, a purpose in one sentence, and a product. A resource identified but not used is only a wasted afternoon.

pyqs.question: Mention different areas of work education. For successful implementation of Work Education in school, what strategies you will adopt?
answer: Work enters a school through five main areas.

- Subject-based work, growing out of what a subject is already teaching — geometry giving measurement and folding, science giving magnetism and simple electricity, language giving the reading aloud and the dictation.
- Local specific work, drawn from the occupations, materials and crops of the locality — bamboo and cane work, pottery, weaving, vegetable growing, food preservation, repair.
- Daily institutional work: cleaning of classroom and compound, the garden, the mid-day meal and the assembly, each on a rotating roster with boys and girls alike.
- Graded workshop and vocational exposure, with complexity rising with the class — tearing paper, then folding a file cover, then binding a register.
- Community and project work — exposure visits, a survey of local vocations, and the curricular project.
For implementation I would adopt these strategies.

- Plan it and grade it. Every activity needs a written plan, a materials list, a division of labour and a safety note. A single demonstration teaches almost nothing; a graded, term-long programme changes children.
- Integrate rather than add. One activity should carry objectives from several subjects, so that no separate work period is needed — otherwise work education has already reintroduced the division it exists to end.
- Build it on local resources and local people, recording for each a person, a date, a purpose and a product.
- Consult before deciding. A measure imposed on teachers without asking them is resented and does not survive the term.
- Assess with the right tool — a skill by performance, an attitude by observation over time — and publish the criteria before the work begins.
- Keep dated records of counts, weights and costs. A checked and recorded task improves; an unrecorded one decays.

pyqs.question: Mention two short comings in evaluation of work education at school level and give suggestions for their elimination.
answer: Two shortcomings account for most of what goes wrong when a school evaluates its work education.

First, evaluation is almost entirely written and terminal. Marks are given twice a year for answers in prescribed books, and a written answer cannot show whether a child can actually sow a row, stitch a straight seam or cook a dish. The consequence is worse than unfairness: a week of honest work in the garden is worth nothing, so children learn quickly that the work period does not count. The remedy is to bring the work into the internal assessment with its weighting announced in advance, to examine the product itself, and to hold at least one practical demonstration per term. The child makes a tray, sows a row or cooks a dish from start to finished product, and the product is kept as evidence.

Second, no criteria are published and no record is kept. The child is judged against a standard never told to it, and because nothing is written down, growth cannot be shown and last year's work cannot be compared with this year's. The remedy is to publish the rubric or checklist before the work begins, keep a portfolio and a register, and give the record back to the child — a child who can see four dated photographs of the same bed as it grew has been assessed by something honest.

Neither remedy costs money. Put together they give a workable scheme: a short record after every activity, the product examined, one demonstration a term, a child-owned portfolio, self and peer assessment against published criteria, and a parent meeting with the child present. The skill lies in matching the tool to the claim — using a written test to judge a stitching skill is not assessment, it is a guess.

practice: What is curricular integration?
Curricular integration connects learning across subjects through a meaningful theme, problem or activity.
Give one mathematics concept used in making a paper box.
Measurement of length.
Give one language activity connected with a work project.
Writing clear instructions for completing the project.
What is a material resource?
A material resource is a physical item used for learning or work, such as paper, clay or a suitable tool.
What is a learning portfolio?
A learning portfolio is a purposeful collection of work and reflections showing a learner's progress over time.
What is an assessment checklist?
A checklist records whether specified observable features or actions are present.
What is a rubric?
A rubric describes criteria and levels of performance used to assess and explain the quality of work.
What is process assessment?
Process assessment examines how a learner plans, performs and reviews a task.
What is product assessment?
Product assessment examines the qualities of the completed outcome, such as whether a made object serves its purpose.
What is formative feedback?
Formative feedback gives information during learning that helps the learner improve a next step.
Give two links between gardening and environmental studies.
Learners observe plant growth and the conditions needed for it.
They examine responsible use of water and suitable reuse of organic material in a supervised activity.
Give two links between a work project and language learning.
Learners discuss plans and explain decisions to one another.
They write a sequence of steps or a report describing what they did and learned.
State two reasons for using local materials.
Suitable local materials can reduce cost and make an activity easier to organise.
They connect learning with familiar surroundings and invite discussion of local knowledge and resource use.
Give two considerations when inviting a community expert.
The person's knowledge should suit the learning goal and they should understand the learners' age and needs.
The school should agree on safe activities, respectful arrangements and appropriate supervision in advance.
Distinguish a checklist from a rating scale.
A checklist records the presence or absence of a specified action.
A rating scale indicates its degree or quality, such as how consistently a learner follows an agreed procedure.
State one strength and one limitation of teacher observation.
It reveals actual behaviour while learners work, including cooperation and use of materials.
It can miss events or be influenced by the observer's expectations, so clear criteria and repeated observations are needed.
State one strength and one limitation of a portfolio.
It can show development through successive work samples and reflections.
It requires purposeful selection and review; a collection of attractive items alone may not show who did the work or what was learned.
Why should assessment criteria be explained before an activity?
Learners understand what matters, such as planning, safe practice and cooperation, not only appearance.
Clear criteria also support useful self-assessment and more transparent feedback.
What can oral questioning reveal during a practical task?
It can show whether the learner understands why a step or material was chosen.
It can also reveal reasoning about a difficulty that the final product alone does not explain.
Give two ways parents can support a school work project without making the product for the child.
Share relevant experience or suitable reusable materials voluntarily.
Discuss the child's plan and encourage reflection while leaving age-appropriate decisions and making to the learner.
Explain three criteria for choosing a locally relevant project.
It should address a meaningful learning goal and connect with learners' surroundings.
Required materials, time and supervision should be feasible and safe.
All learners should have an accessible way to participate, without depending on unequal purchases or help from home.
Explain how making a cloth bag can integrate different subjects.
Mathematics: measure pieces and estimate the amount of material needed.
Language: describe the making process through instructions or an oral explanation.
Environmental studies: compare reuse with disposal and discuss how a durable bag can reduce repeated material use.
State three roles of the head teacher in a work-education project.
Provide time, coordination and approval for a feasible learning plan.
Arrange appropriate resources and supervision, including safe community involvement.
Review participation and learning with teachers and support improvements when barriers arise.
How can teachers identify a school problem suitable for a project?
Observe the setting and invite learners' and staff members' views about recurring difficulties.
Choose a manageable problem that offers learning opportunities, such as disorganised reading materials.
Check that the proposed student role is safe and educational; structural repairs and other specialist work belong to competent adults.
Explain three weaknesses of assessing only the finished product.
It may overlook reasoning, cooperation and safe habits developed during the activity.
It may reward adult help or purchased work rather than the learner's own performance.
It can disadvantage beginners whose learning is substantial even though their first product is imperfect.
Suggest three kinds of evidence for a group project assessment.
Teacher observations of each learner's participation and practical decisions.
Plans, draft versions and the completed work showing how the group developed its solution.
Individual explanations or reflections so a shared product does not conceal differences in understanding.
How can self-assessment be used after a work activity?
Give learners a few clear criteria, such as planning materials and completing an agreed role.
Ask them to identify evidence of a strength and a difficulty rather than merely awarding themselves a score.
Help them choose an achievable improvement and compare it with teacher feedback.
Explain how peer assessment can remain constructive.
Use specific shared criteria focused on work and behaviour rather than personal popularity.
Model respectful comments that identify evidence and suggest a next step.
Monitor the process and combine peer feedback with other evidence; peers should not publicly rank or ridicule classmates.
What should a report on a community resource visit include?
The purpose, setting and relevant people or materials observed.
A clear account of what learners investigated and how it connects with school learning.
Reflection on participation, safety, difficulties and how a future visit could be improved.
Why should assessment tools be combined?
Each tool reveals a different aspect: observation shows actions while questioning reveals reasons.
Work samples show outcomes and progress, but may not explain the level of help provided.
Using complementary evidence gives a fairer judgement than relying on a single score or impression.
Design a simple rubric for a classroom materials-organising project.
Planning: judge whether the learner identifies useful categories and explains the arrangement.
Practical work: judge appropriate handling, labelling and placement of materials.
Cooperation: judge contribution, listening and fair sharing of roles.

Review: judge whether the learner checks that the arrangement is usable and suggests an improvement. Describe levels such as 'with support' and 'independently' for each criterion so the rubric guides feedback.
A local artisan offers a demonstration using tools unsuitable for young children. How should the teacher adapt the opportunity?
Agree with the artisan on the learning goal and identify which processes learners can observe safely.
Arrange adult handling of hazardous tools and clear supervision; local expertise does not remove the need for school safeguards.
Provide an accessible alternative, such as exploring a weaving pattern with paper strips, so learners can practise the related idea safely.
Follow the activity with questions and reflection connecting the demonstration and adapted task. Respect the artisan's expertise while retaining responsibility for appropriate learner participation.
Plan assessment during a plant-growing project.
Before starting, identify criteria such as explaining plant needs, caring regularly and recording observations.
During the project, observe individual actions and ask learners to explain choices.
Collect brief records showing changes and responses to problems, not only the healthiest final plant.
Give feedback and review what was learned. Consider differences in starting materials and conditions so the assessment does not reward luck or resources alone.
Explain four ways to make work-education assessment fairer.
Use clear criteria linked to intended learning and explain them in accessible language.
Provide suitable materials and adaptations so learners have fair opportunities to demonstrate learning.
Gather evidence of each learner's process and understanding, including the assistance received.
Assess progress and give actionable feedback rather than judging only polish, cost or speed. Review inconsistent judgements with additional evidence.
Show how one classroom project can address a real problem and several subjects.
Problem: learners find it difficult to locate books in a shared collection.
Work task: organise and label books, designing a usable borrowing arrangement with support.
Subject links: count and classify books in mathematics, write labels and instructions in language, and discuss shared responsibility in social learning.
Review use of the collection and revise the arrangement. The project is integrated because the subject learning helps solve the problem.
Develop an integrated project using safe reusable materials.
Choose a useful outcome, such as a labelled stationery organiser, and discuss the problem it should solve.
Select clean, safe materials available to all learners and plan supervised methods suitable for their age.
Connect designing with measurement and shape, and connect planning and reporting with language learning.
Let learners share roles, test the organiser and revise its design using evidence about stability and usability.
Assess the process and result through observation, explanation and reflection. Discuss resource use and possible improvements rather than rewarding decoration alone.
Discuss the advantages and limitations of five assessment tools for work education.
Observation captures real actions but can miss events; use clear criteria and several occasions.
A checklist is quick for specific behaviours but gives little detail about quality or reasons.
A rubric describes quality more clearly, but its levels must be understandable and applied consistently.
A portfolio shows development over time, but needs purposeful selection and evidence of the learner's own work.
Oral questioning reveals understanding, but responses may be affected by language or anxiety. Use accessible prompts and combine tools to reach a balanced judgement.
Plan collaboration between teachers, parents and community members for a work activity.
Teachers identify learning goals and consult families about relevant knowledge and practical constraints.
Agree on a suitable activity and voluntary contributions, avoiding assumptions that every family can provide materials or time.
Clarify roles: teachers guide learning, community members share expertise and parents support arrangements where appropriate.
Plan access, supervision and safe methods before learners participate, keeping responsibility for the educational programme with the school.
Review learners' experiences and outcomes with participants, thank contributors and use feedback to improve future collaboration.
Explain how assessment can improve learning rather than merely produce a mark.
Define what learners should understand and be able to do so observations have a clear purpose.
Gather evidence during the task, allowing misconceptions or difficulties to be identified while improvement is still possible.
Give specific feedback about an effective action and a manageable next step.
Provide time to use the feedback and encourage learners to explain what changed.
Review progress with fresh evidence and adjust teaching. A final mark may summarise performance, but the ongoing feedback process is what directly supports further learning.
Critically examine an activity where parents produce most of the submitted models.
The model may be impressive but provides weak evidence of the learner's practical skill or understanding.
It creates unfair differences based on the time, money and expertise available at home.
Teachers should clarify that support may include discussion or arranging suitable materials, while learners do the appropriate work.
Provide supervised school time and assess plans, attempts and explanations so individual learning becomes visible.
Value progress, reasoning and reflection alongside the outcome. This reduces pressure for expensive products and makes assessment more educationally meaningful.

pyqs.question: Write one advantage of domestic budget.
answer: One advantage is that it shows a family exactly where its money goes and which heads can be reduced — food, festivals, fuel and light — so that spending becomes a plan instead of a habit.

pyqs.question: Mention one importance of family budget.
answer: A family budget is important because its value lies in comparison: the first budget a child makes must be a record of one full month, and the plan for the next month is then set against what actually happened.

pyqs.question: Write a short note: Household safety and security.
answer:
Household safety and security
Safety is the prevention of injury, security is the protection against loss, and maintenance is the routine work that keeps the first two effective — a fire drill is safety, a locked door is security, oiling a jammed hinge is maintenance. Most household accidents come from small unrepaired defects: an open well, a loose step, an exposed wire, medicine left within reach.

pyqs.question: What should be the roles and responsibilities of family members in the caring of elderlys sick person?
answer:
For the sick: know the name of the illness and where the doctor is, keep the room clean, aired and quiet, fetch water and medicines, prepare simple food, read to the patient, and keep a relative's telephone number at hand.
For the old: listen and remember what they say, read and write letters, help with the post, sit with them when the household is busy, and notice food, medicine, hearing, a fall risk or a bulb that has failed. The loneliness of the old usually harms them more than their physical need.

pyqs.question: How can we avoid misuse of natural resources? Give three suggestions.
answer: Do not moralise children into saving; measure them into it. A child who has filled a bucket and watched twenty litres disappear in ten minutes will not need to be told again.

1. Measure first, then set a target. Count the drips from a tap in one minute and multiply by 1440 to get the daily loss. Read the electricity meter on the same date every month, weigh the firewood used in a week, and note the tank level at the same hour each week.

2. Repair and reduce at the source. Mend every leaking tap and put a bucket under a drip to measure it; close taps while brushing teeth and use a mug instead of a running tap; use the minimum bulb power that will do and switch off lights on leaving a room; cook in one lidded pot with the fire sized to the pot.

3. Harvest and reuse, not merely use less. Fix a gutter and a leaf filter along the roof edge, lead the water to a drum for the garden, and pipe the overflow into a soak pit layered coarse below and fine above, left open to percolate. In Assam the point is not only less use but storage and recharge, since the rain falls in about four months and the rest of the year is dry.

pyqs.question: “Work education helps students to be responsible towards family and society” — Explain.
answer: Responsibility is not taught by telling a child to be responsible. It is built out of jobs the child genuinely owns, each with a record, a deadline and a consequence.

Towards family, work education produces three habits. First, sharing household work - a time chart filled in for one working week, shared by time rather than by importance, with every member given a share that is theirs alone, including the repair and the planning and not only the sweeping. Second, keeping a budget for a full month and comparing it with what actually happened, with the saving taken first and not last. Third, care - helping younger children, fetching water and medicine for the sick, and sitting with the old, whose loneliness is usually more damaging than their physical need.

Towards society the same habits widen. A group garden, a school bank or a boundary clean-up teaches that the school's property belongs to the community, and keeping the tool register and the accounts teaches accountability. Naming the cook, gardener, sweeper and watchman as members of the school raises a child who will one day take responsibility for others instead of merely obeying.

pyqs.question: Why preparation of budget for the family is important? Mention the steps of preparing a domestic budget.
answer: A family budget matters because money remembered is money already spent. Without one, the household finds at the month's end that festivals and social obligations have eaten the year's savings, and it borrows. A budget shows where the money really goes, names the largest items, and turns hope into numbers a child can act on.

The steps are:
- Fix the period as one full month.
- Enter every item of income, including irregular, seasonal and in-kind income at its money value.
- Enter expenditure under clear heads - food, housing, education, health, transport, fuel and light, clothing, festivals.
- Total each head and the month, and note the three largest items.
- Set the saving aside first, on the day the income comes in.
- Plan the next month against the record, and compare the plan with what actually happened.

pyqs.question: What is the necessity of budget in a family? Prepare a model budget for middle class family.
answer: A budget is necessary because a family that does not write its money down discovers at the end of the month that the money went anyway. It shows where the income actually goes, so the largest item can be planned instead of merely suffered. It exposes the item most often left out — festivals, gifts and social obligations — which is the commonest cause of borrowing at the year end. It protects the item that must never be cut, which is education. It turns saving from whatever is left over, which is nothing, into a fixed sum taken out on the day the income arrives. And it gives children economic awareness: a child who has kept the petty cash and knows what a kilogram of seed costs can say what would happen if the selling price fell.
A model monthly budget for a middle class family of four with an income of ₹40,000:

Total income — ₹40,000
- Food — ₹12,000 (30%)
- Housing and maintenance — ₹6,000 (15%)
- Education — ₹4,800 (12%)
- Transport — ₹3,200 (8%)
- Festivals and social obligations — ₹3,200 (8%)
- Savings — ₹3,200 (8%)
- Clothing — ₹2,800 (7%)
- Health and medicine — ₹2,400 (6%)
- Fuel and light — ₹2,400 (6%)

Savings stand at eight per cent here rather than the ten of the rural model, because a middle class household carries a fixed housing cost and medical risk; where the income is secure, the share can be raised. The discipline is the same in both cases — write it down, save first, and then compare this plan with what actually happened, because a budget is only useful against the record of a real month.

pyqs.question: What is domestic budget? Prepare a model budget for your family?
answer: A domestic budget is a written statement of what a household expects to receive in a stated period and what it plans to spend on, kept in a form in which it can be compared with what actually happened. That last clause is what makes it more than a wish-list. Money remembered is money already spent, so it has to be written down; and a child's first budget should be a record of one real month, not a plan for an imaginary one, with every item of income entered — including irregular, seasonal and in-kind income at its money value.
A model monthly budget for a household of five in rural Assam:

Total income — ₹15,000
- Food — ₹5,250 (35%)
- Housing, water and sanitation — ₹1,800 (12%)
- Festivals, gifts and social obligations — ₹2,100 (14%)
- Education — ₹1,200 (8%)
- Transport — ₹900 (6%)
- Health and medicine — ₹750 (5%)
- Clothing — ₹750 (5%)
- Fuel and light — ₹750 (5%)
- Savings — ₹1,500 (10%)

Food takes the largest share in a rural household, and the family's own kitchen garden is what brings it down. Festivals and social obligations are the item most often left unplanned, and the commonest single cause of borrowing at the year end. Education is the one that must never be the item cut.

Three habits make the budget work, and all three can be taught to a nine-year-old. Write it down. Save first — the saving is taken out on the day the income arrives, not whatever is left at the end of the month, because saving last is saving nothing. And compare: the value of a budget is not the budget itself, but the comparison of the plan with the record, repeated for the next month.

practice: What is a household responsibility?
It is a task or duty that contributes to the care and functioning of a home and its members.
What is a fixed household expense?
It is an expense that usually remains the same over a given budgeting period, such as a fixed monthly rent.
What is a variable household expense?
It is an expense whose amount can change between budgeting periods, such as expenditure on transport.
Define saving in a household budget.
Saving is the part of income set aside rather than spent during the budgeting period.
What is a budget deficit?
A budget deficit occurs when planned or actual expenditure exceeds income for the period.
Give one example of a household need.
Safe drinking water.
Give one example of resource conservation at home.
Turning off an unused light conserves electricity.
What is preventive maintenance?
Preventive maintenance is timely care or repair intended to stop damage or failure before it becomes a larger problem.
Give one suitable responsibility for a young child at home.
Putting their own books in an agreed place, with support as needed.
What does respectful care involve?
Respectful care responds to a person's needs while preserving their dignity, preferences and appropriate independence.
Why should household work be shared without gender bias?
All family members benefit from the home and can contribute through suitable responsibilities.
Sharing work fairly develops practical competence and avoids placing an unequal burden on one gender.
Distinguish needs from wants when planning expenditure.
Needs are essential for basic living and responsibilities, such as food and necessary schooling expenses.
Wants are desirable but can often be postponed or reduced; the distinction helps prioritise limited income.
Why should a budget include an allowance for unexpected expenses?
Some expenses, such as an urgent repair, do not occur regularly but can disrupt a plan.
Setting aside a feasible amount makes the budget more resilient and reduces the need for sudden cuts to essential spending.
Give two ways to involve children in simple budgeting.
Use fictional amounts to plan a small activity and compare the cost of possible materials.
Ask children to check the total and explain a choice, without requiring disclosure of private family income.
State two respectful ways to support an older family member.
Ask what assistance they would find useful rather than assuming they cannot manage tasks.
Offer companionship or help with suitable everyday activities while respecting privacy and choices.
Give two ways learners can help conserve water safely.
Use only the water needed for a task and turn taps off properly.
Report leaks to a responsible adult so they can be repaired; children should not attempt unsafe repairs.
