Give two ways to reduce unnecessary electricity use.
Switch off lights or fans when they are not needed, where the learner can do so safely.
Use available daylight for suitable activities and tell an adult about faulty equipment instead of handling damaged wiring.
Why should household chores suit a child's age and abilities?
A suitable task allows useful participation without exposing the child to avoidable danger or unreasonable strain.
It also provides an achievable learning experience while leaving time for education, rest and play.
What is the value of recording actual expenditure?
It shows where money was really spent rather than relying on memory.
Comparing it with the plan helps identify differences and prepare a more realistic next budget.
Give two ways to keep shared living spaces easier to use.
Return items to agreed places so family members can find them and move through the space.
Keep commonly used paths clear and report hazards to an adult rather than leaving them for someone else to encounter.
Explain three principles for sharing household tasks fairly.
Consider each person's age, ability, available time and existing responsibilities.
Avoid allocating tasks by gender or treating one member's work as automatically less important.
Discuss and review the arrangement so duties can change when needs or circumstances change.
Outline three stages of preparing a simple monthly budget.
Estimate the income available for the month and list essential commitments.
Allocate amounts for needs, other planned expenses and feasible savings, checking that the total fits the income.
Record actual spending and review differences before preparing the next plan.
A fictional family has ₹20,000 income and ₹18,500 planned spending. Calculate the balance and suggest how to use the result.
The balance can be assigned to savings or an identified future need rather than treated as automatically available for extra spending.
Check that essential and irregular expenses have been included before finalising the plan; this is an educational example, not a universal household budget.
How can a family adjust a budget when income temporarily falls?
Recalculate the income available and identify essential expenses first.
Review postponable or reducible spending and discuss fair adjustments with family members.
Track the revised plan and seek suitable support if essential needs cannot be met, rather than presenting all financial difficulty as careless spending.
Suggest three non-medical ways to support a sick family member.
Offer companionship and listen to what support the person wants.
Help with agreed everyday tasks, such as bringing suitable items or keeping their space comfortable.
Tell a responsible adult about concerns and leave treatment decisions to caregivers and qualified professionals; children should not take on adult nursing responsibilities.
Explain how caring for others can develop social responsibility.
It makes learners attentive to needs beyond their own convenience.
Suitable shared tasks develop cooperation and reliability.
Reflection connects helpful action with dignity and mutual support, avoiding the idea that a person receiving care has no say in decisions.
How can a family reduce waste when buying household goods?
Check existing supplies and prepare a list before shopping.
Choose quantities that can be used rather than buying more simply because of an offer.
Review storage and use of items so usable materials are not discarded unnecessarily.
Suggest a classroom activity about conserving household resources.
Use a fictional household scenario showing unnecessary use of water, electricity or materials.
Ask groups to identify feasible changes and explain why each would help.
Have learners create a short reminder plan and review it without requiring them to expose private family habits.
Why does household maintenance require planning?
Regular checks can identify small problems before they disrupt daily life.
Planning helps allocate time, money and appropriate adult or professional help.
Clear responsibility also prevents unsafe attempts by children and avoids assuming that one family member must handle every repair.
Explain how domestic work can support learning without becoming exploitation.
Tasks should be safe, age-appropriate and limited, with adult guidance.
They should develop useful habits and shared responsibility rather than replace necessary adult labour.
Participation must not interfere with schooling, rest, play or dignity, and the child's needs should remain central.
Prepare a balanced fictional monthly budget for an income of ₹25,000.
Housing: ₹7,000; food and household essentials: ₹7,000.
Utilities: ₹2,000; transport: ₹2,000; education: ₹2,000.
Health and other necessary expenses: ₹2,000; savings and contingency: ₹3,000.
Total = ₹25,000. These are illustrative allocations, not standard costs; an actual family should adapt the categories and amounts to its income, location and needs.
Explain four ways to support older people without reducing their independence.
Ask about their preferences and the tasks for which they want help.
Offer appropriate practical assistance while allowing them to continue activities they can and wish to manage.
Include them in family conversation and decisions rather than speaking as if they are absent.
Respect privacy and avoid making assumptions from age alone. Support should respond to the individual, with responsible adults handling specialised care needs.
Design a fair household-duty chart for a fictional family.
List recurring tasks such as arranging belongings, preparing meals, cleaning shared spaces and purchasing supplies.
Discuss members' time, abilities and existing workload before assigning suitable responsibilities.
Use rotation where practical and include shared tasks, avoiding labels such as 'boys' work' or 'girls' work'.
Review the chart regularly and adapt it during illness or other changes. Children's tasks should remain safe and limited, and adults retain responsibility for hazardous work.
Explain how careful planning can conserve water, electricity, fuel and materials.
Water: use suitable amounts for tasks and arrange repair of leaks through responsible adults.
Electricity: avoid leaving unnecessary appliances operating and use daylight where practical.
Fuel: plan suitable shared journeys or nearby errands to avoid unnecessary trips, considering safety and access.
Materials: maintain and reuse useful items and buy realistic quantities. Conservation should meet essential needs efficiently, not deny them.
A budget shows repeated overspending. Explain how to review it without blaming family members.
Compare planned and actual amounts to identify which categories differ.
Discuss reasons such as changing prices, overlooked necessities or unrealistic original estimates.
Agree on feasible adjustments and priorities, distinguishing essential needs from postponable spending.
Keep records and review the revised plan together. A budget is a planning tool, not proof that hardship results from individual failure.
Develop a school activity connecting household responsibility with social responsibility.
Begin with a fictional household and ask what tasks make shared daily life possible.
Discuss fair contributions according to age and ability, explicitly questioning gender stereotypes.
Connect the same principles with a suitable school task, such as organising shared learning materials.
Let learners plan roles, carry out the safe task and reflect on how their contribution affects others.
Assess cooperation and thoughtful explanation, not children's private home circumstances. Emphasise that responsible participation includes seeking help and respecting limits.
Explain the complete process of preparing and reviewing a family budget.
Identify the budgeting period and estimate income realistically, noting uncertainty where income varies.
List essential regular expenses and likely irregular commitments rather than relying only on last month's spending.
Allocate available income among priorities and feasible savings, checking the arithmetic and adjusting the plan if it exceeds income.
Record actual expenditure during the period and discuss significant differences respectfully.
Use the records to revise the next budget and respond to changed needs. The process helps make informed choices but cannot by itself solve inadequate income or unexpected hardship.
Plan a classroom lesson on caring for family members respectfully.
Use an age-appropriate fictional situation involving a family member who needs everyday assistance.
Ask learners to identify the person's preferences and needs rather than assuming that care means taking over all decisions.
Discuss suitable supportive actions such as companionship or help with simple agreed tasks, while leaving medical and hazardous responsibilities to adults and professionals.
Use role-play to practise asking permission, listening and offering help without pity or ridicule.
Reflect on dignity, boundaries and shared responsibility. Do not require disclosure of learners' private family or health situations.
Explain how a resource-conservation project can avoid becoming only a poster competition.
Choose a specific, observable issue in the school, such as paper being discarded after one-sided use.
Record a simple starting picture of the issue without collecting unnecessary personal information.
Plan a feasible change, such as a box for suitable reusable paper, with clear responsibility.
Try the change and review whether materials are actually reused and whether any access or hygiene concerns arise.
Use a poster only to communicate the agreed practice. Learning comes from investigating, acting and evaluating, not from decoration alone.
Discuss the relationship between self-reliance and mutual care in family life.
Self-reliance develops through managing suitable responsibilities, such as organising one's belongings.
Mutual care recognises that people also depend on one another and may need different kinds of support.
Fair sharing prevents independence from being confused with expecting everyone to manage without help.
Respectful communication allows family members to state needs and contribute according to their abilities and circumstances.
Together, these principles support a household in which people act responsibly and assist one another without humiliation, rigid gender roles or unreasonable burdens on children.
